 This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Kunal Bahl, the 43-year-old cofounder of the Indian digital commerce holding company AceVector Limited and investment firm Titan Capital. It has been edited for length and clarity. 
 Entrepreneurship was always on the cards for me. An H-1B rejection just fast-tracked it.
 I grew up in New Delhi, and then I went to the University of Pennsylvania in the US for a program that blended an engineering and business degree.
 While I was in college, a bunch of big things happened in the tech sphere: Google went public, and Facebook became viral. By 2006, which is when I graduated, it was all the rage.
 The internet economy was taking off. I had a lot of business ideas, but it became clear that I could not start a company because of my visa status. I was on an F-1 visa , and I first needed to find an employer who could sponsor my H-1B, then lay out a pathway into Silicon Valley. From there, I'd try to start my own company.
 I interned at Microsoft during my junior year and returned in October 2006 in a full-time role after graduating.
 Then my H-1B visa petition was rejected
 While waiting for my H-1B visa selection, I was counting down the days until my Optional Practical Training , a temporary yearlong work authorization after graduation, would expire.
 I remember vividly that, in June or July of 2007, I got an email that said my H-1B petition had been rejected.
 For a moment, I didn't understand. It was unfathomable to me that, if I worked at a company like Microsoft, my H-1B visa would not be approved.

 I checked with the Microsoft team. Looking at their faces, I gathered that there was a finality to the rejection .
 The company was very nice about the situation, suggesting that I work in the Microsoft India office and try again for the H-1B after a year.
 At no point had I considered moving back to India . But I gathered myself up and decided that if I go back to my country, I'd work for myself, not for Microsoft.
 No time wasted starting my company
 I no longer had the baggage of having to figure out this H-1B situation. I felt liberated because I didn't have to worry about visas or green cards.
 So I called up my best friend from high school, Rohit Bansal, who was working in a financial institution at the time. We used to sit next to each other in class and talk about starting a business together. I asked if he wanted to do something together.
 He said, "Great, let's do it."
 Our company was incorporated on September 12, 2007, a few days before I touched down in India.
 Building a startup in India in 2007 was a challenge
 India has a hot startup ecosystem now. That cannot be said of the India of 2007.
 The country had very few internet users and smartphones, and digital payments were few and far between. Things were pretty dull, to be honest. I was not returning to the promised land or a burgeoning startup ecosystem.
 Even launching a startup was frowned upon. People would ask, "You guys have a good education, so why didn't you get a job? Does nobody want to hire you?"
 We started as a physical coupon book business, because Indians love a good value. But getting funding was a challenge. Angel investors weren't common then.
 We had both saved up a bit from our year working corporate jobs and pooled our savings — about $60,000 in total. That became our seed capital.
 We stayed with our families for food and accommodation, and worked out of a small office in the basement of a residential building in Delhi's furniture market. We had neighbors complain about people going in and out of the building late, because Rohit and I would work 20 hours a day to get our business off the ground.
 Our company pivoted from being an online couponing platform like Groupon to one of India's first e-commerce platforms, called Snapdeal. Now we have two publicly listed companies that we spun off from the original coupon book business.
 We wanted to give back to the startup ecosystem in India, as well. In 2011, once we had built up some capital, we started investing in early-stage startups and formed Titan Capital .
 Over the last 15 years, we've invested in more than 320 startups, many of which have gone public. I'm now also a judge on Shark Tank India.
 The India of today is full of opportunity
 In hindsight, my not getting the H-1B visa was serendipitous, though it hurt at the time. It was part of a larger plan: I had to return to India and help the next generation of founders.
 It was easy for me to pack up my bags and come back because I wasn't married and didn't have children. And I know it's far more difficult for those who have dependents living with them in the US, like children or parents.
 So I do empathize with workers facing immigration struggles in the US.
 That said, India has changed drastically since the time we started our company.
 India now has a billion internet users. There's ubiquitous smartphone penetration. There are so many coworking spaces for startup founders. There is a high talent density.
 There is a robust funding ecosystem. The startup tech scene is front of mind for the government.
 There is no better time to come back to India.
